result: Human participants failed to discriminate between temporal odor mixtures (TOMs) composed of orange and cinnamon presented in different temporal orders at delays of 300 ms and 600 ms. At Δt=300 ms, 9/10 participants performed at chance level (median success rate=0.55, p=0.51), and at Δt=600 ms, 7/9 participants failed (median=0.5, p=1). Performance was significantly lower than all control conditions where odor content differed.
evaluation: Claims C23, C27-C30, C34-C35 provide converging evidence with appropriate statistical tests (binomial tests, t-tests, sign tests, ANOVA with post-hoc comparisons) and adequate sample sizes. The control experiments (C31-C33) demonstrate that poor performance was specific to TOMs and not due to experimental limitations. The statistical rigor and consistency across multiple delays support this result.

result: When tested with more dissimilar odors (citral and dimethyl trisulfide), the majority of participants (88%, 38/43) still failed to discriminate between TOMs across all tested delays (75, 150, 300, and 600 ms). Group median success rates were not significantly above chance for Δt=75 and 150 ms, and only marginally significant for Δt=300 and 600 ms.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37 demonstrate that even with perceptually more distinct odors (C74 shows CTL/DMTS distance was significantly higher than ORG/CIN), participants still failed to discriminate TOMs. The large sample size (43 participants) and consistent pattern across multiple delays strengthen this finding. This addresses a potential confound that similar odors might explain the initial negative results.

result: Extensive training over 200 trials (5 sessions) did not improve discrimination of TOMs. Mean success rates ranged from 0.51-0.64 across sessions and did not improve significantly as a function of session number (p>0.05 in 4/5 sessions).
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 provide evidence that the failure to discriminate TOMs is not due to insufficient training or practice. The longitudinal design with monetary incentives addresses motivation concerns. Statistical tests appropriately show no learning effect. This is important for ruling out that temporal coding could be exploited with sufficient experience.

result: TOMs were perceived as intermediate percepts between their constituent odors rather than as distinct odors. At both Δt=300 ms and Δt=600 ms, the perceptual distance between the two TOMs (AB vs BA) was significantly smaller than the distance between constituent odors (A vs B): for 300 ms, 10.11±3.48 vs 14.24±4.09 (p=7.35E-18, Cohen's d=1.08); for 600 ms, 10.98±3.39 vs 18.86±4.33 (p=2.61E-13, Cohen's d=1.25).
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 provide direct perceptual evidence using verbal descriptor ratings and PCA analysis. The statistical comparisons with large effect sizes (Cohen's d>1) and highly significant p-values strongly support that TOMs are perceived similarly regardless of temporal order. This directly addresses whether temporal order creates distinct percepts, which is central to evaluating temporal coding models.

result: When participants were explicitly informed that TOMs were composed of two consecutive odorants, discrimination performance improved significantly as a function of delay. For ORG/CIN, there was a significant main effect of Δt (F(3,44)=6.05, p=0.0015), and for CTL/DMTS, F(3,28)=19.94, p<0.00001. However, performance remained near chance for delays <150 ms.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46, C52 demonstrate that temporal information can be extracted when participants are aware of the stimulus structure, but this does not reflect spontaneous odor perception. The ANOVA results with large effect sizes (partial eta-squared 0.292-0.681) are statistically robust. The failure at short delays suggests limitations in temporal resolution or pattern matching strategies (C54-C55). This dissociates extractable temporal information from odor percept per se.

result: Participants could easily discriminate between a TOM and one of its constituent odors, and between TOMs when one component was replaced with clean air or a different odor. Success rates were high: A vs (A/B) median=0.9 (p=0.0156), B vs (A/B) median=0.84 (p=0.0156), AB vs (AB/AC) median=0.75 (p=0.004), AB vs (AB/BC) median=0.9 (p=0.031).
evaluation: Claims C24, C31-C33 provide essential control experiments demonstrating that poor TOM discrimination is not due to experimental limitations, inadequate ISI, or inability to discriminate the constituent odors. The high success rates with strong Bayesian support (BF10>100) validate the experimental paradigm. These controls are critical for interpreting the main negative results.

result: The authors conclude that glomeruli activation times do not elicit a prominent difference in odor percept, but can be used to extract temporal odor information such as detecting the order of odor delivery in a sequence. Latency coding could be utilized to extract odor-related information without substantially affecting odor perception.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C56, C65 represent the main conclusions drawn from the experimental findings (C23-C46). The distinction between odor percept and extractable temporal information is supported by the contrast between spontaneous discrimination (failed) and informed discrimination (succeeded). This interpretation is logically consistent with the data, though the mechanistic basis remains speculative.

result: The results are more consistent with one interpretation of the Laurent model (time is not necessarily part of the code) than with the Hopfield model (time is part of the code), and do not align with temporal coding models where first-activated glomeruli form the odor code.
evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide a theoretical interpretation of the experimental results in the context of existing models. The logic is sound: if temporal order created distinct percepts (as Hopfield predicts), participants should have discriminated TOMs easily. The failure to discriminate, combined with perceptual similarity (C40-C43), supports the Laurent interpretation. However, alternative interpretations of the Hopfield model remain possible (acknowledged in the discussion).

result: PID measurements validated precise odor delivery with onset latency of 20-40 ms and offset within 30-50 ms. All TOMs elicited similar response dynamics, with highly consistent odor concentrations across trials of the same condition. The order of odor presentation was preserved at the participant's nose location (~5 cm from ports), though concentration was more variable at this distance.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67, C99-C104 provide technical validation of the odor delivery system using objective PID measurements. This addresses potential concerns about stimulus control and demonstrates that the experimental manipulation (temporal order) was successfully implemented. The acknowledgment of increased variability at 5 cm is appropriate. These measurements are essential for interpreting the behavioral results.

result: Control experiments confirmed that constituent odors had similar perceived intensities (ORG vs CIN: p=0.66; CTL vs DMTS: p=0.43) and that participants showed no response bias (similar error rates for 'same' vs 'different' trials: p=0.92).
evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C75 provide important controls ruling out intensity differences and response bias as confounds. The statistical tests are appropriate (paired t-tests) with adequate sample sizes. These controls strengthen the interpretation that poor discrimination reflects genuine perceptual similarity rather than experimental artifacts.

result: Respiratory phase analysis showed that TOMs were encountered at correlated phases between first and second presentations (correct trials: r=0.67, p=1.33E-8; incorrect: r=0.549, p=1.02E-5), but phase differences did not differ between correct and incorrect trials (p=0.236).
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 address whether respiratory phase contributed to discrimination performance. The circular statistics are appropriate for phase data. The lack of difference between correct and incorrect trials rules out phase-dependent discrimination strategies. This control is important given that phase coding is one variant of temporal coding models.

result: Methodological decisions were justified: switching TOM order creates substantial differences in glomerular activation times (±Δt shift); 8 s ISI was used because longer intervals impaired performance even for constituent odors by converting the task to working memory; 20 trials per participant minimized sensory fatigue while remaining within standard practice.
evaluation: Claims C68-C71 provide methodological justifications supported by pilot data (C69) and citations to standard practices (C71). The logic for the 8 s ISI is sound and addresses a potential criticism. The inference about glomerular activation time differences (C68) is reasonable given the experimental design. These justifications strengthen confidence in the experimental choices.

result: The perceptual distance between CTL and DMTS was significantly higher than between ORG and CIN (5.52±1.12 vs 4.18±1.25, p=3.1E-8, Cohen's d=1.12), confirming that the second odor pair was more dissimilar.
evaluation: Claim C74 validates the choice of CTL/DMTS as a more dissimilar odor pair using verbal descriptor ratings and Euclidean distance calculations. The large effect size and highly significant p-value support this characterization. This is important for interpreting why even dissimilar odors failed to produce discriminable TOMs.

result: Data quality control procedures excluded 73 participants (leaving 284) and 8.3% (CIN/ORG) to 5.6% (CTL/DMTS) of trials based on respiratory synchronization criteria. Participants with <14 valid trials (70% of session) were excluded. Results remained unchanged with less stringent criteria.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79, C94, C105-C106 describe appropriate data quality control procedures with clear exclusion criteria. The sensitivity analysis (C106) showing results remain unchanged with different criteria strengthens confidence in the findings. The exclusion rates are reasonable and transparently reported. This demonstrates methodological rigor.

result: The authors speculate that improved discrimination at longer delays when participants were aware of TOM structure might be due to: (1) detection of a pause between odors when delays were introduced, or (2) pattern-matching strategies where participants searched for specific odors at the beginning or end. Pattern matching failed at delays <150 ms due to temporal overlap.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are explicitly speculative interpretations of the awareness experiment results (C44-C46). While the speculation is reasonable and consistent with participant reports (C54), there is no direct experimental evidence distinguishing between these mechanisms. The authors appropriately present these as possible explanations rather than established findings. Additional experiments would be needed to test these hypotheses.

result: The authors speculate that temporal coding may be part of the odor code in macrosmatic animals (rodents, insects) and that temporal dynamics can be utilized under extreme conditions. They note that mouse optogenetic studies demonstrated use of timing but did not prove mice perceived stimuli as different odor percepts—mice may have perceived same odor at different respiratory phases or as different durations.
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 are explicitly speculative (C57, C60-C62) or interpretations of others' work (C58-C59). While the reinterpretation of mouse optogenetic studies (C59) is insightful, it remains speculative without direct evidence. The speculation about macrosmatic animals (C57) is reasonable but untested. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work but are not supported by data in this manuscript.

result: Detailed methodological descriptions of stimuli (odor compositions, dilutions), apparatus (custom olfactometer, respiration recording, PID measurements), experimental parameters (stimulus duration 200 ms, ISI 8 s, ITI 23 s), participant characteristics (284 total, 191 female, 93 male, ages 18-41, normosmic, healthy), and procedures (rating protocols, ethical approvals, exclusion criteria).
evaluation: Claims C80-C119 provide comprehensive methodological details that are internally consistent and follow standard practices in olfactory psychophysics. The GCMS analysis of fragrant oils (C82-C83), equipment specifications, and procedural details enable reproducibility. Ethical approvals (C112-C113) and participant characteristics (C114-C119) are appropriately documented. These are standard methodological descriptions.

result: Background on olfactory system organization: odor perception starts with odorant-receptor binding; different odorants bind to overlapping receptor sets; in rodents, each olfactory sensory neuron expresses one receptor and projects to one glomerulus; each odorant activates a unique set of glomeruli; this led to the spatial/identity code hypothesis, which is theoretically capable of encoding any number of odors.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 summarize established knowledge about olfactory system organization, supported by appropriate citations (C3, C5, C6) or presented as general knowledge (C1-C2, C4, C7). These provide necessary background context for understanding the experimental rationale. The characterization of this prior work appears accurate based on the citations provided.

result: Background on the Hopfield latency coding model and supporting evidence: odors are encoded by neuron identity and activation time relative to oscillatory cycles; the model provides concentration-invariant recognition; two odors activating similar glomeruli at different times should evoke distinguishable percepts. Supporting evidence includes stimulus-specific glomerular latency patterns in rodents, concentration effects on onset times, latency coding in Xenopus larvae, downstream neuron sensitivity to relative timing, and mouse behavioral discrimination of optogenetic stimuli differing in timing.
evaluation: Claims C8-C17 accurately summarize the Hopfield model (C8-C10) and cite appropriate supporting evidence from the literature (C11-C17). The citations appear relevant and the characterization of prior work is fair. This background is essential for establishing the theoretical motivation for the experiments. The authors appropriately distinguish between different variants of latency coding (phase, latency from onset, relative timing).

result: Background on the Laurent model: populations of neurons exhibit synchronized oscillatory activity with transient participation; neuron identities participating in oscillatory ensembles change over time, forming odor representations that are gradually decorrelated; temporal dynamics are not necessarily part of the odor code but facilitate coding optimization. Supporting evidence includes observations of evolving dynamics, increasing sparseness and decorrelation over time, and impaired discrimination when gamma oscillations are disturbed.
evaluation: Claims C18-C22 accurately summarize the Laurent model with appropriate citations (C18-C22). The characterization distinguishes this model from the Hopfield model and notes the key difference in the role of temporal dynamics. The supporting evidence is appropriately cited. This provides necessary theoretical context for interpreting the experimental results.

result: Background context: substantial odor information can be extracted from sub-sniff neuron spike timings, but whether temporal dynamics in rodent odor-elicited neural responses are part of the odor code remains an ongoing debate.
evaluation: Claims C63-C64 provide appropriate context from the literature (C63 with multiple citations) and accurately characterize the current state of the field (C64). This framing motivates the experimental approach of testing temporal coding in humans where perceptual reports are possible.
